cards.definition: The Ancient Greek theory that the body contained four fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — and that illness was caused by an imbalance between them.
An Ancient Greek physician who rejected supernatural explanations for illness and promoted clinical observation, rest and diet as treatments.
A Roman physician whose ideas dominated medicine for over 1,000 years. He developed the theory of opposites and made important anatomical discoveries, though some were wrong.
Galen's treatment method — if a patient had too much of one humour, they were given the opposite, e.g. a cold, wet remedy for a hot, dry illness.
The belief that disease was caused by bad air from rotting matter. It was wrong about the cause but led to some useful public health improvements.
In the Middle Ages, the Catholic Church controlled education and medicine. It supported Galen's ideas and discouraged dissection, slowing medical progress.
Islamic scholars such as Ibn Sina preserved and developed Greek medical knowledge during the medieval period, producing influential medical texts.
An Islamic physician whose book 'The Canon of Medicine' was used across Europe for centuries. He linked disease to soil and water contamination.
Run by the Church and focused on prayer and care rather than cure. They isolated the sick but rarely provided effective medical treatment.
A devastating plague that killed around one third of Europe's population in the 14th century. It was blamed on bad air, sin and Jewish people — not bacteria.
A 16th-century Belgian anatomist who proved Galen wrong about human anatomy through dissection, publishing his findings in 'The Fabric of the Human Body' (1543).
A 17th-century English physician who proved that blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart — disproving Galen's theory that blood was constantly produced.
Invented by Gutenberg in the 15th century, it allowed new medical ideas to spread quickly across Europe, challenging old Galenical teaching.
The incorrect belief that disease and living things could arise from non-living matter — e.g. maggots from rotting meat. Disproved by Pasteur.
Louis Pasteur's 1861 discovery that microorganisms (germs) cause disease and decay, replacing miasma theory and revolutionising medicine.
A French chemist who proved germ theory, developed the rabies vaccine and pioneered pasteurisation — one of the most important figures in medical history.
A German scientist who identified specific bacteria causing tuberculosis, cholera and anthrax, linking individual germs to individual diseases.
Using a weakened or dead form of a disease to stimulate the immune system. Edward Jenner pioneered the first vaccine for smallpox in 1796.
An English physician who developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796 after observing that milkmaids who caught cowpox did not get smallpox.
A 19th-century nurse who transformed hospital hygiene during the Crimean War, dramatically reducing death rates and professionalising nursing.
The first antibiotic, discovered accidentally by Alexander Fleming in 1928 when mould killed bacteria in a petri dish. Developed into a treatment by Florey and Chain.
A Scottish scientist who discovered penicillin in 1928. His discovery led to the development of antibiotics, saving millions of lives.
The National Health Service, founded in 1948, providing free healthcare for all in the UK — a major step in improving public health regardless of wealth.
In 1953, Watson and Crick (using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data) discovered the double helix structure of DNA, transforming understanding of genetics and disease.
Specific chemical treatments designed to target and kill particular microbes without harming the patient — pioneered by Paul Ehrlich with Salvarsan (1909).
Controlled tests used to assess whether new treatments are safe and effective before they are approved for use with patients.
Modern understanding that diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol are major causes of illness — a shift from treating to preventing disease.
From the 19th century, governments have taken increasing responsibility for public health through clean water acts, vaccination programmes and the NHS.
James Simpson introduced chloroform in 1847 and Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic techniques in 1867, making surgery safer and more survivable.
Medical progress is driven by science and technology, war, government, chance, communication and the role of individuals — rarely by one factor alone.
A state of political tension and military rivalry between the USA and USSR from 1945 to 1991, fought through proxy wars, propaganda and an arms race rather than direct combat.
The US economic system based on private ownership, free markets and democracy — ideologically opposed to Soviet communism.
The Soviet political and economic system based on state ownership, central planning and a one-party state — ideologically opposed to Western capitalism.
A meeting between Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin to plan post-war Europe. Agreements were made over free elections in Eastern Europe, which Stalin later ignored.
A post-war meeting between Truman, Attlee and Stalin that revealed deepening tensions, particularly over reparations and the future of Germany.
A phrase used by Churchill in 1946 to describe the division of Europe between the democratic West and the Soviet-controlled communist East.
The US policy of containing the spread of communism by providing military and economic support to countries threatened by Soviet expansion.
A US programme providing over $13 billion of economic aid to rebuild Western Europe after WWII, aiming to prevent poverty from making communism attractive.
Stalin's attempt to force the Western Allies out of Berlin by blocking all road, rail and canal routes. The West responded with a massive airlift supplying the city.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation — a military alliance of Western nations formed to provide collective defence against Soviet aggression.
The first major proxy conflict of the Cold War, in which US-led UN forces and Chinese troops fought to a stalemate, leaving Korea divided at the 38th parallel.
A revolution in Hungary against Soviet control, crushed by Soviet tanks. The West did not intervene, showing the limits of the Truman Doctrine.
A wall built by East Germany to stop people fleeing to the West. It became the defining symbol of the Iron Curtain and Cold War division.
The most dangerous moment of the Cold War — the USSR placed nuclear missiles in Cuba. After 13 days of tension, a deal was reached and the missiles were removed.
The doctrine that if either superpower launched a nuclear attack, both sides would be destroyed — deterring either from starting a nuclear war.
A period of reform and liberalisation in Czechoslovakia, crushed by Soviet invasion. The Brezhnev Doctrine was used to justify the intervention.
The Soviet policy that the USSR had the right to intervene in any communist country that threatened the stability of the Eastern Bloc.
A period of reduced tension between the superpowers in the 1970s, marked by arms limitation treaties (SALT) and increased diplomatic contact.
Strategic Arms Limitation Talks — agreements between the USA and USSR to limit the number of nuclear missiles each side could hold.
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended detente and triggered the Second Cold War. The USA funded the Mujahideen resistance fighters.

cards.keyword: Reagan and the Second Cold War
cards.definition: US President Reagan increased military spending and introduced the Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI/'Star Wars'), putting pressure on the USSR's struggling economy.
Soviet leader from 1985 who introduced glasnost and perestroika, reducing tension with the West but inadvertently accelerating the collapse of the USSR.
Gorbachev's policy of 'openness' — allowing greater freedom of speech and media in the USSR, which ultimately weakened communist control.
Gorbachev's policy of 'restructuring' the Soviet economy, introducing limited market reforms that destabilised the Soviet system.
The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty between Reagan and Gorbachev — the first agreement to eliminate an entire class of nuclear weapons.
A wave of anti-communist revolutions across Eastern Europe in 1989, as Soviet satellite states broke free. The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989.
On 9 November 1989, the Berlin Wall was opened and then demolished — a powerful symbol of the end of the Cold War and Soviet control over Eastern Europe.
The Soviet Union formally dissolved on 25 December 1991, ending the Cold War. Fifteen new independent states were formed, including Russia.
A conflict where the superpowers supported opposing sides rather than fighting each other directly, e.g. Vietnam, Korea, Afghanistan.
The competition between the USA and USSR to build more and better nuclear weapons, driven by mutual fear and the logic of deterrence.
Queen of England from 1558 to 1603. She navigated religious division, foreign threats and court politics to establish a long and relatively stable reign.
Elizabeth's compromise between Catholicism and Protestantism — the Church of England became Protestant but kept some Catholic features to avoid religious conflict.
Elizabeth's most important advisory body, made up of senior nobles and officials who helped govern the country and implement royal policy.
Elizabeth used Parliament to pass laws and raise taxes, but clashed with it over religion, marriage and the succession — she disliked parliamentary interference.
Elizabeth's Catholic cousin who was seen as a rival claimant to the English throne. She was kept under house arrest for 19 years before being executed in 1587.
Refusing to attend Church of England services. Catholics who refused faced fines; later in Elizabeth's reign they faced more severe punishments.
Extreme Protestants who wanted to 'purify' the Church of England of remaining Catholic influences. Elizabeth kept them under control but did not satisfy their demands.
Pope Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth, declaring it was not a sin to murder her. This increased pressure on English Catholics and made them seem disloyal.
The system by which Elizabeth rewarded loyal courtiers with titles, land and positions — a key tool for managing the nobility and maintaining loyalty.
Elizabeth's refusal to marry or name a successor was a major source of tension with Parliament. It gave her diplomatic power but created uncertainty about the future.
Philip II of Spain sent a fleet of 130 ships to invade England. It was defeated by a combination of English tactics, fireships and storms — a major propaganda victory for Elizabeth.
The Catholic king of Spain and Elizabeth's main foreign enemy, who launched the Armada in 1588. His motives were religious, political and personal.
The Earl of Essex, a former royal favourite, attempted an uprising against Elizabeth's government. It failed immediately and Essex was executed.
Rising poverty in the late 16th century led to the Poor Law (1601), which made parishes responsible for supporting the poor — an early example of state welfare.
Elizabethan explorers like Francis Drake and Walter Raleigh expanded English trade and founded early colonies, increasing national wealth and prestige.
An English sea captain who circumnavigated the globe (1577-80), raided Spanish ships and ports and was knighted by Elizabeth — seen as a hero or pirate depending on perspective.
Elizabethan theatre flourished, with playwrights such as Shakespeare and Marlowe writing for a broad public audience at venues like The Globe.
Women in Elizabethan society had limited rights and were expected to be obedient to fathers or husbands. Elizabeth's queenship was unusual and required careful management of gender expectations.
The problem of 'masterless men' — unemployed, homeless men wandering the country — was seen as a major social threat and was addressed through increasingly harsh laws.
Elizabeth's reign is seen as a golden age of culture, exploration and stability. However, she left no heir and many of her problems — poverty, Ireland, religious tension — remained unsolved.
The democratic government of Germany from 1919 to 1933, named after the city where its constitution was written. It was politically weak and faced constant opposition.
The peace treaty that ended WWI. Germany lost territory, was forced to pay reparations, accept the War Guilt Clause and severely limit its military.
Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, which forced Germany to accept full blame for WWI. It was deeply resented and used by extremists to undermine the Weimar government.
The Weimar voting system that gave parties seats in proportion to their vote share. It led to coalition governments and political instability.
A catastrophic collapse of the German currency caused by the government printing money to pay striking workers during the Ruhr crisis. Savings became worthless.
Hitler's failed attempt to seize power in Bavaria. It was crushed and Hitler was imprisoned — but the publicity helped him rebuild the Nazi Party.
German foreign minister (1923-29) who stabilised the currency, negotiated the Dawes Plan and restored Germany's international standing during the 'Golden Twenties'.
A global economic crisis triggered by the Wall Street Crash. German unemployment rose to over six million, causing mass poverty and making extremist parties more attractive.
The myth that Germany had been betrayed by politicians and Jews rather than defeated militarily in WWI. Used by the Nazis to undermine the Weimar Republic.
A clause in the Weimar constitution allowing the President to rule by emergency decree. It was increasingly used and later abused, undermining democracy.
The National Socialist German Workers' Party, led by Hitler. It used propaganda, violence and electoral politics to gain power in Germany.
Information designed to promote a political cause or point of view. Goebbels ran the Nazi propaganda machine, controlling newspapers, radio, film and art.
The Nazi paramilitary force who intimidated political opponents, attacked Jews and disrupted rival political meetings. Also known as Brownshirts.
The German parliament building was burned down. Hitler blamed the communists and used it as a pretext to suspend civil liberties with the Reichstag Fire Decree.
A law passed by the Reichstag giving Hitler the power to make laws without parliamentary approval for four years — effectively ending democracy in Germany.
Hitler ordered the murder of SA leaders, including Ernst Rohm, to remove a potential rival and secure the loyalty of the army.
The title meaning 'leader' that Hitler gave himself in 1934, after combining the roles of President and Chancellor following Hindenburg's death.
A state where the government has total control over all aspects of life — politics, economy, culture, education and the media.
Hitler's elite personal guard who became a powerful force in the Nazi state, running the concentration camps and carrying out terror and murder.
The Nazi secret police who monitored, arrested and tortured opponents of the regime. They relied heavily on informers within the German population.
A Nazi organisation for young boys aged 14-18, focused on physical training, Nazi ideology and preparation for military service.
The female equivalent of the Hitler Youth, preparing girls for their role as wives and mothers in Nazi Germany.
'Children, kitchen, church' — the Nazi ideal for women, who were expected to focus on the home and family rather than work or politics.
Laws that stripped Jews of German citizenship, banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews and excluded Jews from many aspects of public life.
'Night of Broken Glass' — a coordinated nationwide pogrom against Jews in which synagogues were burned, businesses smashed and nearly 100 Jews killed.
Camps where political opponents, Jews and other 'undesirables' were imprisoned. From 1942, death camps were used to systematically murder Jews in the Holocaust.
The systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others by the Nazi regime, carried out through mass shootings and death camps.
Nazi policies such as rearmament and public works programmes dramatically reduced unemployment from 6 million in 1933 to under 1 million by 1936.
Despite the terror, some Germans did resist — including the White Rose group, army officers involved in the July 1944 bomb plot and some church leaders.
'People's community' — the Nazi idea of a racially pure German national community that excluded Jews, Roma, disabled people and other groups.
